Salt, most famously sodium chloride. An ionic compound formed by the reaction of an acid with a base. In the narrower chemical sense, any ionic compound composed of cations and anions is a salt. In everyday usage, salt refers to table salt, an essential seasoning and electrolyte in food and biology. Salt represents one of the most abundant and economically significant compounds on Earth.

Sodium chloride forms through the reaction of sodium, a highly reactive metal, with chlorine gas, a toxic nonmetal, producing a stable ionic solid held together by electrostatic attractions. Table salt crystallizes in the cubic rock salt crystal structure, where each sodium ion is surrounded by six chloride ions and vice versa, forming an infinitely extended ionic lattice. It dissolves readily in polar solvents like water, dissociating into free sodium and chloride ions that conduct electricity. This ionic dissociation is essential to its role as an electrolyte. Salt comprises approximately 3.5 percent of seawater by mass, making the ocean a vast reservoir of salt. Salt has been harvested from seawater for millennia through evaporation. It is essential to human and animal physiology. Sodium and chloride ions regulate nerve impulses, muscle contraction, and fluid balance across cell membranes. Salt is mined from underground salt deposits, called rock salt or halite, formed by the evaporation of ancient seas. These deposits represent geological records of past marine environments. Salt is a critical industrial chemical, used in food preservation, de-icing, and chlor-alkali processes to produce chlorine and sodium hydroxide, along with countless other applications. Sodium is the metal element that comprises the cation in sodium chloride, joined with chlorine, the nonmetallic anion, through ionic bonding.
